National Health Care Crisis (Hospital Horrors)

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Patients dying on waiting lists, shortages of doctors, nursing staff and beds - and a lack of funds. The state of national health care is in crisis. With NHI pending is there a remedy for the present?

Unique Selling Point:
According to Dr Pat Saffy, head of Emergency at Helen Joseph, COVID has precipitated the national health care crisis South Africans are currently facing. With over two years lost the backlog, for operations and key treatments that could save lives, has become more and more unmanageable, and in addition there are further bed shortages because so many are allocated for COVID patients. The already underfunded, understaffed and overburdened health system is falling apart. Heads of Units, like Dr Saffy, are at their wits end. She does not see the value of R7.7 billion rand being allocated for more vaccines while in the meantime patients are dying awaiting life saving treatment, because of lack of funds. Dr Saffy has in principle agreed to give us the inside track. She feels frustrated and helpless.

Whilst researching this story, 2 possible case studies have already died due to lack of care and possible neglect in the public hospitals they were going to. We have two case studies from Helen Joseph who are currently facing life threatening outcomes without proper and prompt treatment, but they may not get the treatment they need in time. Trying to help them is Faeeza Marshman a community service worker who tirelessly tries to fight for getting people the right help in order to save their lives. She believes that it is poor management and neglect that is impacting the patients so negatively, and that once she gets involved things seem to happen a little faster.

Dr Nicholas Crisp, DDG DOH, who is in charge of the NHI, believes that it is the only solution, but the bill has not been passed yet and it could take a few years. He says the public health system is collapsing because there are no funds, and with budget cuts the prospect of things getting any better is remote. Proponents say the only answer is NHI, which means by allocating the funds spent by the private sector across the national needs, more effective health care will be available for all.

Mike Van Wyk, CEO of Medicare, who runs primary health care centres based on the NHI guidelines and has done his thesis on why the NHI in its current proposed form won’t work, tells us why. He believes there are other solutions but they will only work if the entire NHI is treated as a business.

Summary:
We have received images and stories from across the country of broken hospitals, unkempt and dirty toilets, stories of people waiting for operations, patient neglect, psychiatric patients spending days in chairs in ER’s because there are no beds, deaths of patients due to inadequate care and facilities. We focus on Gauteng and Helen Joseph Hospital, which has had to bear the brunt of COVID, as well as the over flow from a fire at Charlotte Maxeke, but nationally the picture is bleak within the public health care sector. It seems that there is very little light on the horizon. Are people dying as a result of a broken system?

We speak to patients who have lost their quality of life and could lose their lives if not treated soon. We get further insight from community service worker Faeeza Marshman who helps patients trying to get treatment from Helen Joseph.

We turn to the DOH, DDG, Dr Nicholas Crisp, who explains why NHI is the only long term solution, and until that time comes, the department is hamstrung with budget cuts in an already overextended system, that needs a lot more bolstering.

Mike Van Wyk, believes there are solutions, but not in NHI in its current form and proves how he is making primary affordable health care work, and how the NHI is doomed to failure within the first two years if it isn’t run properly.

Dr Pat Saffy, says there is nothing more doctors, nurses and staff can do, when they are working around the clock and having to overcome insurmountable challenges - not enough staff, failing facilities, lack of beds and a Department that doesn’t seem to have the funds to improve anything. (hopefully she will speak and not change her mind)


Further information:
Dr Saffy points out, that to make matters worse in Gauteng, Helen Joseph and surrounding hospitals like Baragwaneth, have had to take on additional patients due to the devastating fire at Charlotte Maxeke hospital. Not only did they have to take on extra patients but no additional budget was supplied to the hospital. Nationally there was a 1.6% budget cut. Already understaffed, at Helen Joseph three out of 15 desperately needed doctors have resigned in the Emergency department, many suffering fatigue and overwork, the DOH is not replacing them. She speaks with desperation on how psychiatric patients have to sit in chairs in the ER for days because there are no beds, they end up a danger to other patients and to themselves, sometimes hospital staff and doctors are also in danger.

In the meantime people are suffering at the hands of the state. Faghmida Bennet is being treated at Helen Joseph, a 48 year old cancer patient in remission, she has had a perforated bladder for over two years, but her operation keeps getting pushed back, so now she is once more, facing a life threatening situation, because she also has a stoma and the urine is leaking from the bladder into the stoma. Her next appointment to be seen by a specialist at Helen Joseph is in October. She has completely lost her quality of life, she used to be an outgoing and gregarious person, now she is afraid to go out. She still has to work but finds it hard to function.
Another Helen Joseph patient, Ighsaan Samsodien finally made it into a theatre after waiting for two years for a stoma to be reversed, but now when the complications have set in, which could be detrimental to his health, like necrotising facitis, he is once again being made to wait and who knows for how long? Due to lack of treatment Igshaan had lost his job because he couldn’t function. Just when he thought he’d get his life back, things are falling apart.

I propose we treat the story putting Helen Joseph forward as a case study and a reflection of what is happening in many hospitals around the country. Other than the overflow from CM, which has made matters worse for the facility, it is indicative of a health care system that is broken down at the core. Who is going to fix it? What is government doing?

DDG Dr Nicholas Crisp, says there is no present solution only NHI and for that we have to wait. But he believes in time it will be the only answer.

There are many who believe it cannot work as it is, Mike Van Wyk states his case. Dr Pat Saffy and he are in agreement that corruption which is endemic in the DOH will persist and prevail in the implementation of NHI, and that a small populous that supports the private healthcare sector cannot subsidise and entire country’s health care. In the end everyone will suffer even more. There are other solutions that could make a shift to more functional public health care.

I am also hoping to get an insider (hidden identity) a top administrator from another hospital who will speak to the maladministration and why that is a primary reason for the malfunction in many public hospitals. (but that has not been confirmed as yet)

Press Release:


What hope for our public hospitals? The severity of the South African Health crisis is marked by relentless suffering, despair and death and it’s wearing our patience thin.

Script:


Faeeza: That hospital is disgusting it's smelly you're too scared to touch anything if they see to a patient they just throw the needles and whatever just there. Sometimes they get food sometimes they don't get food…
VO: Faeeza Marshman, a community service worker in the Bosmont area of Johannesburg, is talking about Helen Joseph hospital, one of Gauteng's busiest and most crucial. It services around a million people and many who need urgent medical attention like 49-year-old cancer survivor Fagmida Bennett.

Fagmida: I'm not comfortable my life is standing still, I don't go nowhere. Im only at home from work - home. I don't go to visit nothing.
VO: Fagmida developed complications after her remission and has been forced to wear diapers for the last four years. Self-conscious, she started isolating herself.

Fagmida: because every time when I go visit, if I stand up, I must look at myself because of the urine it's leaking and I must change myself five to six times a day.
VO: Faeeza has witnessed the untold trauma of the people she's trying to help in her community, and sole breadwinner, Ighsaan Samsodien, is also under her watch. He was diagnosed two years ago with necrotising fasciitis.// This rare flesh-eating disease is life-threatening.
Ighsaan: The beginning of January 2020, they done three major operations. I was left with a stoma bag because I couldn't pass a stool because of a lot of cuts that they do.
Faeeza: and then when he came in explained to me situation as to him Okay, I'll see what I can do to assist you
VO: Both Ighsaan and Fagmida's lives have been put on hold for years, because they can't get the operations they urgently need at the Helen Joseph hospital.
Nicholas: The whole health system is in serious turmoil. And we have a lot of problems in our health system
VO: DDG of the National Department of Health Dr Nicholas Crisp, is responsible for National Health Insurance, NHI, which aims at providing universal access to quality health care for all South Africans. He is fighting to undo the skewed management and funding of health across public and private.
Nicholas: The number of available posts to fill to employ people is getting less because the budget is getting less and the unit cost of the individuals is getting higher. and the number of patients who need to be looked after is getting more and more and more.
VO: People travel from far to get treatment in Gauteng’s big tertiary hospitals but many professionals here feel disillusioned. Without support and funds, eroding standards hit patients hardest
Fagmida: Like every time when I go for my checkup and I just given you a new date new date, new date.
VO: The reasons for long waiting times vary, but Crisp points out that the availability of specialist doctors is disproportionate, 67% work in the private sector.
Nicholas: The numbers of specialists to look after complicated health care conditions in the public sector is very small. The question is, how do we get the public sector-dependent patient to be seen by those same doctors in an equitable manner?

VO: The country spends 8 and a half percent of GDP on healthcare – half of that buys services in the private sector, for only 14% of the population.
Nicholas: What we need to do is find better ways to spend what we have, there's not a shortage of money. There's a very big shortage of efficiencies within the system.
VO: Crisp says the NHI will pool funds from the entire country's annual spend on health care. But can this work if shortcomings are so evident now? // Ighsaan lost his job waiting for treatment.
Ighsaan: I didn't want to see anybody I didn't want to speak to people, even to cuddle my wife just to hold her. I couldn't even do that.
VO: Ighsaan and his wife survived hand to mouth with the help of family and by selling home-cooked meals. Two years had passed without an operation date to remove his colostomy bag. //Until Faeeza intervened. First, she spoke to the hospital administrators.
Faeeza: There's no proper management from the actual quality manager or manager at that hospital. They really don't know what they're doing there.

VO: When she received no joy, she took it all the way to the health ombud. Finally, Ighsaan was operated on in June this year. // After a short recovery unfortunately his illness developed complications which could signal the return of his flesh-eating disease, now, he can't get another operation date.
Ighsaan: If it does come back and start eating and get to my organs, there is nothing they can do for me, then I'm basically gonna die. He's put me on the priority list, however, it can be a wait up to three months.
VO: The challenges keep mounting. In Gauteng, a fire in 2021, at the essential Charlotte Maxeke hospital in Johannesburg, as well as COVID, have put an even bigger strain on hospitals including Helen Joseph. WIth annual budget cuts of around 1.7% and a strangled economy the sector is struggling as it is. But are there other factors fracturing the system?

Mike: We're sitting now with with general managers or CEOs of hospitals that has teaching qualifications, that got nothing to do with healthcare.
VO: Mike Van Wyk is CEO of Medicare 24, a group of clinics focused on affordable medical care. But when it comes to state healthcare he believes there is one key underlying problem. Management!

Mike: You don't need to be a doctor to manage a facility, you need to be a business person that needs to manage the facilities. But with healthcare experience, //
VO: The NHI is supposed to be an equitable solution... provided it’s done properly.// But can government be trusted to do the job? //BEAT// COVID proved to be a great testing ground for the sharing of resources, especially in the development and implementation of the digital system
Nicholas: You've already seen the integration of some of health care services, you're already seeing the purchasing of private services by some of the provincial administrations. But you need a framework of where you're going so that it is legal to do these things.Just getting the bill through Parliament is gonna take a while. So we need at least another year, I would guess.

VO: Government has to get public hospitals and facilities up to speed - to pass quality accreditation so that they qualify for NHI contracts.

Mike: If we do not have the right people in the places from procurement, right through to the operations, right through to the facility management, and people do not take accountability, it will crash.// The UK has run out of funds for their NHI how are we in South Africa and afford NHI.
VO: Ultimately the NHI still has to be funded so how much will it cost?
Nicholas: Eight and a half percent of GDP. That's what it's gonna cost. Close to 500 billion. If you take away all that over-servicing all the duplication in the public and the private sector, all the unnecessary administration, you will easily save 100 Million rand.
Mike: Is it sustainable already we talking about additional taxes. So you're going to get taxed in your personal capacity. Some of your medical aid funds that you claim back on yearly basis, and the employee here is going to pay half of the employees' funds that's going to be used for NHI. So we're talking about billions and billions if that gets lost in the system, or misappropriated, we have a big problem

VO: So the elephant in the room is, what will happen to private medical services?
Nicholas: Everybody thinks that NHI is aiming to get rid of medical schemes. And force everybody who currently has medical aid to go to a government hospital. There's no where in the NHI bill that it says anything like that.
VO: The catch for the medical schemes is that eventually, they will not be able to offer any service the NHI offers.
Nicholas: Forget about the private sector for now In order to get the money into the national health insurance plan to pay for health care, you have to remove the functions from the provinces.
VO: Currently Gauteng has a lot to answer for. On the ground, Faeeza has to fight for her community assisting Fagmida, whose nextappointment has been pushed back by three months.
Faeeza: But I'm going back in next week again, to find it out, to say that is not our initial agreement. And then I'll go back to the ombudsman if they don't do it immediately again. .
VO:We approached Helen Joseph Hospital for some answers.// The Gauteng Department of Health responded that there are challenges to address while continuing to service millions of patients annually - they are working on an intervention plan with various stakeholders.

Nicholas: There are provisions in existing legislation which allow us to do things better than we're doing them now. But you need the management skills to be able to do that.
VO: It could take a decade or more for NHI to be phased in. Tellingly, since the NHI Bill was tabled in 2019 attention has shifted away from the 2026 deadline. But preparations do carry on in Crisp’s department, with news that it’s to recruit 44 experts to oversee planning.
Nicholas: You do it over a long period of time. And you start in those phases with primary health care, working on the public sector first, then integrating the private sector it did in bits and pieces.

Nicholas: In my lifetime, it won't get fixed, there's an opportunity to fix it, you have to start now fixing the things that we have broken.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 10 August 2022 Press Release: What hope for our public hospitals? The severity of the South African Health crisis is marked by relentless suffering, despair and death and it’s wearing our patience thin. Script: Faeeza: That hospital is disgusting it's smelly you're too scared to touch anything if they see to a patient they just throw the needles and whatever just there. Sometimes they get food sometimes they don't get food… VO: Faeeza Marshman, a community service worker in the Bosmont area of Johannesburg, is talking about Helen Joseph hospital, one of Gauteng's busiest and most crucial. It services around a million people and many who need urgent medical attention like 49-year-old cancer survivor Fagmida Bennett. Fagmida: I'm not comfortable my life is standing still, I don't go nowhere. Im only at home from work - home. I don't go to visit nothing. VO: Fagmida developed complications after her remission and has been forced to wear diapers for the last four years. Self-conscious, she started isolating herself. Fagmida: because every time when I go visit, if I stand up, I must look at myself because of the urine it's leaking and I must change myself five to six times a day. VO: Faeeza has witnessed the untold trauma of the people she's trying to help in her community, and sole breadwinner, Ighsaan Samsodien, is also under her watch. He was diagnosed two years ago with necrotising fasciitis.// This rare flesh-eating disease is life-threatening. Ighsaan: The beginning of January 2020, they done three major operations. I was left with a stoma bag because I couldn't pass a stool because of a lot of cuts that they do. Faeeza: and then when he came in explained to me situation as to him Okay, I'll see what I can do to assist you VO: Both Ighsaan and Fagmida's lives have been put on hold for years, because they can't get the operations they urgently need at the Helen Joseph hospital. Nicholas: The whole health system is in serious turmoil. And we have a lot of problems in our health system VO: DDG of the National Department of Health Dr Nicholas Crisp, is responsible for National Health Insurance, NHI, which aims at providing universal access to quality health care for all South Africans. He is fighting to undo the skewed management and funding of health across public and private. Nicholas: The number of available posts to fill to employ people is getting less because the budget is getting less and the unit cost of the individuals is getting higher. and the number of patients who need to be looked after is getting more and more and more. VO: People travel from far to get treatment in Gauteng’s big tertiary hospitals but many professionals here feel disillusioned. Without support and funds, eroding standards hit patients hardest Fagmida: Like every time when I go for my checkup and I just given you a new date new date, new date. VO: The reasons for long waiting times vary, but Crisp points out that the availability of specialist doctors is disproportionate, 67% work in the private sector. Nicholas: The numbers of specialists to look after complicated health care conditions in the public sector is very small. The question is, how do we get the public sector-dependent patient to be seen by those same doctors in an equitable manner? VO: The country spends 8 and a half percent of GDP on healthcare – half of that buys services in the private sector, for only 14% of the population. Nicholas: What we need to do is find better ways to spend what we have, there's not a shortage of money. There's a very big shortage of efficiencies within the system. VO: Crisp says the NHI will pool funds from the entire country's annual spend on health care. But can this work if shortcomings are so evident now? // Ighsaan lost his job waiting for treatment. Ighsaan: I didn't want to see anybody I didn't want to speak to people, even to cuddle my wife just to hold her. I couldn't even do that. VO: Ighsaan and his wife survived hand to mouth with the help of family and by selling home-cooked meals. Two years had passed without an operation date to remove his colostomy bag. //Until Faeeza intervened. First, she spoke to the hospital administrators. Faeeza: There's no proper management from the actual quality manager or manager at that hospital. They really don't know what they're doing there. VO: When she received no joy, she took it all the way to the health ombud. Finally, Ighsaan was operated on in June this year. // After a short recovery unfortunately his illness developed complications which could signal the return of his flesh-eating disease, now, he can't get another operation date. Ighsaan: If it does come back and start eating and get to my organs, there is nothing they can do for me, then I'm basically gonna die. He's put me on the priority list, however, it can be a wait up to three months. VO: The challenges keep mounting. In Gauteng, a fire in 2021, at the essential Charlotte Maxeke hospital in Johannesburg, as well as COVID, have put an even bigger strain on hospitals including Helen Joseph. WIth annual budget cuts of around 1.7% and a strangled economy the sector is struggling as it is. But are there other factors fracturing the system? Mike: We're sitting now with with general managers or CEOs of hospitals that has teaching qualifications, that got nothing to do with healthcare. VO: Mike Van Wyk is CEO of Medicare 24, a group of clinics focused on affordable medical care. But when it comes to state healthcare he believes there is one key underlying problem. Management! Mike: You don't need to be a doctor to manage a facility, you need to be a business person that needs to manage the facilities. But with healthcare experience, // VO: The NHI is supposed to be an equitable solution... provided it’s done properly.// But can government be trusted to do the job? //BEAT// COVID proved to be a great testing ground for the sharing of resources, especially in the development and implementation of the digital system Nicholas: You've already seen the integration of some of health care services, you're already seeing the purchasing of private services by some of the provincial administrations. But you need a framework of where you're going so that it is legal to do these things.Just getting the bill through Parliament is gonna take a while. So we need at least another year, I would guess. VO: Government has to get public hospitals and facilities up to speed - to pass quality accreditation so that they qualify for NHI contracts. Mike: If we do not have the right people in the places from procurement, right through to the operations, right through to the facility management, and people do not take accountability, it will crash.// The UK has run out of funds for their NHI how are we in South Africa and afford NHI. VO: Ultimately the NHI still has to be funded so how much will it cost? Nicholas: Eight and a half percent of GDP. That's what it's gonna cost. Close to 500 billion. If you take away all that over-servicing all the duplication in the public and the private sector, all the unnecessary administration, you will easily save 100 Million rand. Mike: Is it sustainable already we talking about additional taxes. So you're going to get taxed in your personal capacity. Some of your medical aid funds that you claim back on yearly basis, and the employee here is going to pay half of the employees' funds that's going to be used for NHI. So we're talking about billions and billions if that gets lost in the system, or misappropriated, we have a big problem VO: So the elephant in the room is, what will happen to private medical services? Nicholas: Everybody thinks that NHI is aiming to get rid of medical schemes. And force everybody who currently has medical aid to go to a government hospital. There's no where in the NHI bill that it says anything like that. VO: The catch for the medical schemes is that eventually, they will not be able to offer any service the NHI offers. Nicholas: Forget about the private sector for now In order to get the money into the national health insurance plan to pay for health care, you have to remove the functions from the provinces. VO: Currently Gauteng has a lot to answer for. On the ground, Faeeza has to fight for her community assisting Fagmida, whose nextappointment has been pushed back by three months. Faeeza: But I'm going back in next week again, to find it out, to say that is not our initial agreement. And then I'll go back to the ombudsman if they don't do it immediately again. . VO:We approached Helen Joseph Hospital for some answers.// The Gauteng Department of Health responded that there are challenges to address while continuing to service millions of patients annually - they are working on an intervention plan with various stakeholders. Nicholas: There are provisions in existing legislation which allow us to do things better than we're doing them now. But you need the management skills to be able to do that. VO: It could take a decade or more for NHI to be phased in. Tellingly, since the NHI Bill was tabled in 2019 attention has shifted away from the 2026 deadline. But preparations do carry on in Crisp’s department, with news that it’s to recruit 44 experts to oversee planning. Nicholas: You do it over a long period of time. And you start in those phases with primary health care, working on the public sector first, then integrating the private sector it did in bits and pieces. Nicholas: In my lifetime, it won't get fixed, there's an opportunity to fix it, you have to start now fixing the things that we have broken.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Patients dying on waiting lists, shortages of doctors, nursing staff and beds - and a lack of funds. The state of national health care is in crisis. With NHI pending is there a remedy for the present?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: According to Dr Pat Saffy, head of Emergency at Helen Joseph, COVID has precipitated the national health care crisis South Africans are currently facing. With over two years lost the backlog, for operations and key treatments that could save lives, has become more and more unmanageable, and in addition there are further bed shortages because so many are allocated for COVID patients. The already underfunded, understaffed and overburdened health system is falling apart. Heads of Units, like Dr Saffy, are at their wits end. She does not see the value of R7.7 billion rand being allocated for more vaccines while in the meantime patients are dying awaiting life saving treatment, because of lack of funds. Dr Saffy has in principle agreed to give us the inside track. She feels frustrated and helpless. Whilst researching this story, 2 possible case studies have already died due to lack of care and possible neglect in the public hospitals they were going to. We have two case studies from Helen Joseph who are currently facing life threatening outcomes without proper and prompt treatment, but they may not get the treatment they need in time. Trying to help them is Faeeza Marshman a community service worker who tirelessly tries to fight for getting people the right help in order to save their lives. She believes that it is poor management and neglect that is impacting the patients so negatively, and that once she gets involved things seem to happen a little faster. Dr Nicholas Crisp, DDG DOH, who is in charge of the NHI, believes that it is the only solution, but the bill has not been passed yet and it could take a few years. He says the public health system is collapsing because there are no funds, and with budget cuts the prospect of things getting any better is remote. Proponents say the only answer is NHI, which means by allocating the funds spent by the private sector across the national needs, more effective health care will be available for all. Mike Van Wyk, CEO of Medicare, who runs primary health care centres based on the NHI guidelines and has done his thesis on why the NHI in its current proposed form won’t work, tells us why. He believes there are other solutions but they will only work if the entire NHI is treated as a business.
metadata.Summary: We have received images and stories from across the country of broken hospitals, unkempt and dirty toilets, stories of people waiting for operations, patient neglect, psychiatric patients spending days in chairs in ER’s because there are no beds, deaths of patients due to inadequate care and facilities. We focus on Gauteng and Helen Joseph Hospital, which has had to bear the brunt of COVID, as well as the over flow from a fire at Charlotte Maxeke, but nationally the picture is bleak within the public health care sector. It seems that there is very little light on the horizon. Are people dying as a result of a broken system? We speak to patients who have lost their quality of life and could lose their lives if not treated soon. We get further insight from community service worker Faeeza Marshman who helps patients trying to get treatment from Helen Joseph. We turn to the DOH, DDG, Dr Nicholas Crisp, who explains why NHI is the only long term solution, and until that time comes, the department is hamstrung with budget cuts in an already overextended system, that needs a lot more bolstering. Mike Van Wyk, believes there are solutions, but not in NHI in its current form and proves how he is making primary affordable health care work, and how the NHI is doomed to failure within the first two years if it isn’t run properly. Dr Pat Saffy, says there is nothing more doctors, nurses and staff can do, when they are working around the clock and having to overcome insurmountable challenges - not enough staff, failing facilities, lack of beds and a Department that doesn’t seem to have the funds to improve anything. (hopefully she will speak and not change her mind)
metadata.Further information: Dr Saffy points out, that to make matters worse in Gauteng, Helen Joseph and surrounding hospitals like Baragwaneth, have had to take on additional patients due to the devastating fire at Charlotte Maxeke hospital. Not only did they have to take on extra patients but no additional budget was supplied to the hospital. Nationally there was a 1.6% budget cut. Already understaffed, at Helen Joseph three out of 15 desperately needed doctors have resigned in the Emergency department, many suffering fatigue and overwork, the DOH is not replacing them. She speaks with desperation on how psychiatric patients have to sit in chairs in the ER for days because there are no beds, they end up a danger to other patients and to themselves, sometimes hospital staff and doctors are also in danger. In the meantime people are suffering at the hands of the state. Faghmida Bennet is being treated at Helen Joseph, a 48 year old cancer patient in remission, she has had a perforated bladder for over two years, but her operation keeps getting pushed back, so now she is once more, facing a life threatening situation, because she also has a stoma and the urine is leaking from the bladder into the stoma. Her next appointment to be seen by a specialist at Helen Joseph is in October. She has completely lost her quality of life, she used to be an outgoing and gregarious person, now she is afraid to go out. She still has to work but finds it hard to function. Another Helen Joseph patient, Ighsaan Samsodien finally made it into a theatre after waiting for two years for a stoma to be reversed, but now when the complications have set in, which could be detrimental to his health, like necrotising facitis, he is once again being made to wait and who knows for how long? Due to lack of treatment Igshaan had lost his job because he couldn’t function. Just when he thought he’d get his life back, things are falling apart. I propose we treat the story putting Helen Joseph forward as a case study and a reflection of what is happening in many hospitals around the country. Other than the overflow from CM, which has made matters worse for the facility, it is indicative of a health care system that is broken down at the core. Who is going to fix it? What is government doing? DDG Dr Nicholas Crisp, says there is no present solution only NHI and for that we have to wait. But he believes in time it will be the only answer. There are many who believe it cannot work as it is, Mike Van Wyk states his case. Dr Pat Saffy and he are in agreement that corruption which is endemic in the DOH will persist and prevail in the implementation of NHI, and that a small populous that supports the private healthcare sector cannot subsidise and entire country’s health care. In the end everyone will suffer even more. There are other solutions that could make a shift to more functional public health care. I am also hoping to get an insider (hidden identity) a top administrator from another hospital who will speak to the maladministration and why that is a primary reason for the malfunction in many public hospitals.
